OBITUARY REFERENCES 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, I re fere with profound sorrow to 
the passing away of Shrimati Pushpalata Das and Shri D.Y Pawar, former 
Members of this House. 
Shrimati Pushpalata Das passed away on the 9th November, 2003 
at the age of 88 years. Born at North Lakhimpur, Assam, in March, 1915, 
Shrimati Das had her education at Banaras Hindu University and Andhra 
university. Shrimati Das was associated with the Quit India Movement 
and was jailed alongwith her husband. She was also associated with 
social welfare work and was closely associated with Mahatma Gandhi. 
Shrimati Das represented the State of Assam in this House for two 
onsecutive terms from April, 1952, to April, 1956, and again from April, 
956, to April, 1962. In 1967, she wa s elected to the Assam Legislative 
assembly. In the passing away of Shrimati Das, the country has lost a 
distinguished social worker and a noted parliamentarian. 
Shri D.Y. Pawar passed away on the 23rd November, 2003, at the 
age of 82 years. Born at Borgabn, District Nasik in 1922, Shri Pawar had 
his education at Daily College, Indore and Elphinston-College, Mumbai. 
A social and political worker, Shri Pawar was actively associated with 
various social and cultural organisations. He was also associated with 
sports activities. Shri Pawar took keen interest in the upliftment of the 
backward classes. 
Shri Pawar represented the State of Maharashtra in this House for 
four terms, from April, 1952 to April 1956, from April, 1956 to April, 1962, 
from April, 1962 to April, 1968, and again from April, 1972 to April, 1978. 

RAJYA SABHA [15 December, 2003] 
In the passing away of Shri Pawa r, the country has lost an aminent 
Parliamentarian. 
We deeply mourn the passing away of Shrimati Pushpalata Das and 
Shri D.Y. Pawar. I request Members to rise in their places and observe 
silence as a mark of respect to the memory of the departed. 
(Hon. Members then stood in silence for a minute) 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Secretary-General will convey to the members of 
the bereaved families our deep sense of sorrow and sympathy.

RAJYA SABHA [15 December, 2003] 
Declaring Carpenters as SC 
†*181. SHRI KRIPAL PARMAR: Will the Minister of SOCIAL 
JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether some MPs from Himachal Pradesh as well as some 
members of the State Assembly repeatedly requested for declaration of 
carpenters as SC as in case of black smiths of that State; 
(b) if so, the details thereof, and 
(c) what is the present status in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF SOCIAL JUSTICE AND EMPOWERMENT 
(DR. SATYANARAYAN JATIYA): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the 
Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) Some Members of Parliament and the Himachal Pradesh 
Assembly have recommended inclusion of the Tarkhan community in 
the list of Scheduled Castes in Himachal Pradesh. 
The proposal was recommended by the Government of Himachal 
Pradesh and as per approved modalities, referred to by this Ministry to 
the Registrar General of India. After receipt of comments from the Registrar 
General of India, it will be possible to  take further .action. In view of 
article 341 (2) of the Constitution of India, the amendment in the list of 
Scheduled Castes can be made only by an Act of Parliament and as 
such, in this regard it is not possible to assign any definite time frame.

Free treatment for AIDS 
*192. SHRI B.J. PANDA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that India has the second largest number of 
patients of HIV/AIDS; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that there is growing demand from the 
public that Government should provide free treatment for this disease, 
as it is not within the reach of a patient of average means; and 
(c) whether any proposal is under Government's consideration to 
offer free or subsidized treatment to the patients, it so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI 
SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
(a) The annual sentinel surveillance conducted by NACO revealed 
that the estimated number of people living with HIV is upto 4.58 million 
in 2002. 
(b) and (c) People living with HI V/AIDS experience a variety of 
health and social support needs as their illness progress and 
opportunistic infections occur. For management of such cases, 
Government has taken following initiatives: (i) Provision of drugs for the 
treatment of opportunistic infections in  all public sector hospitals; (ii) 
Linkages with the Revised National Tuberculosis Programme for early 
diagnosis and treatment of HIV - TB  co-infection; (iii) Provision of 
antiretroviral drugs for post exposure prophylaxis to health care workers 
in case of accidental occupational exposure; (iv) Provision of anti-retroviral

drug (Nevirapine) for prevention of parent to child transmission of HIV; 
(v) Promotion of community and home based care through community 
care centres; and (vi) Involvement of networks of people living with HIV/ 
AIDS in community and home based care to minimize stigma and 
discrimination. 
However, as the disease advance s, occurrence of opportunistic 
infections becomes overwhelming due to the steady deterioration in the 
responses of the human immune syst em. At his stage, antiretroviral 
treatment becomes essential to improve the quality of life and longevity, 
as well as to enable productive and useful living. Government is aware 
that there is a growing demand fo r anti retroviral drugs among people 
living with HIV/AIDS. Due to budgetary constraints, and limitations for 
provisioning of anti retroviral therapy through the public health care system, 
it has not been possible to introduce anti retroviral therapy for AIDS 
patients in India. 
However, Government is now actively contemplating expansion of 
this ongoing programme of care and support for people living with HIV/ 
AIDS across the six high prevalence States, so as to include anti-retroviral 
drugs for specific target groups, through the public health care system.

Incentives for units in SEZ 
184. SHRIMATI BIMBA RAIKAR: Will the Minister of COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to extend additional incentives for 
setting up of units in the Special Economic Zones through a five year 
exemption from Provident Fund/Empl oyees State Insurance liabilities 
for the entrepreneurs; 
(b) whether it is also proposed to relax labour laws and trade union 
Acts to attain higher and committed productivity;and 
(c) whether Government expect t hat these incentives would spur 
growth of the existing SEZs and also the new ones coming up especially 
in Padubidri in Dakshina Kannada region? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (SHRI SATYABRATA MOOKHERJEE): (a) to (c) A 
Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) The Special Economic Zones (SEZs) scheme aims to provide an 
internationally competitive duty free environment for export production 
 16 

[15 December, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
with a simplified procedural framewor k. To achieve this objective, a 
package of incentives/facilities supported by a singly window clearance 
mechanism at the zone level have been put in place. Towards this direction, 
recently the Ministry of Labour has decided that in respect of SEZs, the 
State Government may apply for exemption to the Central Government 
under Section 16(2) of the Employees' Provident Fund and Miscellaneous 
Provisions Act, 1952, from the applicability of the provisions of the Act 
to SEZ for 5 years. The decision shall be taken on case-to-case basis. 
In respect of the ESI Act, 1948, the State Government, being the 
appropriate Government, may take a decision as per the powers provided 
under the Act. 
(b) Normal labour laws which are enforced by the State Governments 
are equally applicable to Special Ec onomic Zones. Exemption if any 
made under the provisions of labour laws will also apply to SEZs. 
(c) The incentives/facilities offe red to the SEZs would help in 
promoting exports from the existing SEZs and also from SEZs approved 
for establishment in the country, including Karnataka.

supply conditions. Similarly, prices also vary from month to month 
depending upon the offtake of the cement.

Statement-ll (See below) indicates that the production in the month of 
November, 2003 over the production of November, 2002 has increased 
by 4.31% and during the period from April to November, 2003 over the 
coresponding period of 2002 it had increased by 4.51%, both of which 
are comparable. 
The present production and price trends do not indicate existence of 
any cartel and the Government has also not received any complaint in 
this regard.

Objectionable advertisements on T.V. 
*188. SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: Will the Minister of 
INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) the steps his Ministry and the Advertising Standards Council of 
India (ASCI) are taking under the Cable TV Regulation Act and the code 
prescribed by the ASCI in order to check the menace of objectionable 
advertisements on TV channels; 
(b) whether it is a fact that recently a meeting was held between the 
ASCI and his Ministry to deal with this issue; and 
41 

RAJYA SABHA [15 December, 2003] 
(c) if so, the outcome thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF INFORMATION 
AND BROADCASTING (SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD): (a) to (c) 
Advertisements, when transmitted/re transmitted, through the cable 
network, are required to adhere to the provisions of the Advertising Code, 
prescribed under the Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995 
and rules framed thereunder. The Central Government has constituted an 
Inter-ministerial Committee under section 20 of the Cable Television 
Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995, to look into the violations of the 
Advertising Code. The Chairman, Advertising Standards Council of India 
(ASCI) is also a member of this Committee. Cognizance of any violation 
of Advertising Code is taken suo-moto or on receipt of a specific complaint 
by the Committee. Show cause notices are issued in the first instance to 
TV channels telecasting objectionable advertisements in violation of the 
provisions of the Advertising Code, and after examination of each case, 
the concerned TV channels are directed not to telecast or retelecast 
advertisements which are found to be in violation of the Code. This is a 
continuous process. On the advice of the Ministry, Indian Broadcasting 
Foundation (IBF) is coordinating with all its members to maintain self-
regulation in broadcast of advertisements. 
The ASCI, a voluntary self-regulatory council, has a notified a code 
for self regulation in advertising, which is to be observed by all who 
commission create place or publish any advertisement or assist in the 
creation or publication of any advertisement. The Code applies to all 
advertisements read, heard or viewed in India. The ASCI has constituted 
a Consumer Complaints Council (CCC) to deal with complaints received 
from consumers and industry against advertisements. During the year 
2002-03, the Council considered 136 complaints and upheld 78 
complaints. 
The last meeting of the Inter-ministerial Committee was held in June, 
2003 and on its recommendations, orders were issued to concerned TV 
channels to stop telecast of advertisements of various kinds pertaining 
to non-liquor products of liquor manufacturing companies and obscene/ 
vulgar advertisements of other products.

(c)  and (d) (i) The Government of India supported the Government 
of Uttaranchal to conduct 2 rounds of Pulse Polio Immunization 
Campaign in the entire State of Uttaranchal during January and

the State of Uttaranchal is supported through a network of 
Surveillance Medical Officers (SMOs) of National Polio 
Surveillance Project (NPSP, which is a joint GOI-WHO project). 
The SMOs of NPSP provide tech nical and logistic support to 
the Government system to ensure detection of the wild 
poliovirus circulation anywhere in the State.

ensure that all infants receive polio drops as a part of the routine 
immunization in addition to the doses that they received during

Doha Declaration on the TRIPS Agreement and Public Health recognized 
that the TRIPS Agreement does not and should not prevent Members 
from taking members to protect public health. It reaffirmed the right of 
WTO Members to use, to the full, the provisions in the TRIPS Agreement 
which provide flexibility for this purpose.The Declaration recognized that 
these facilities include the right of each Member to grant compulsory 
license and the freedom to determine the grounds upon which such license 
is granted, the right to determine what constitutes a national emergency 
or other circumstances of extreme urgency and the freedom to establish 
its own regime for exhaustion of intellectual property rights.

Members with insufficient or no manufacturing capacities in the 
pharmaceutical sector in making effective use of compulsory licensing 
under the TRIPS Agreement and instructed the Council for TRIPS to find 
an expeditious solutions to this problem.

TRIPS Agreement and Public Health. The Decision allows manufacture 
and export of patented pharamaceutical products under a compulsory 
licence to countries with limited or no manufacturing capacities in the 
pharmaceutical sector. This decision would enable countries with limited 
or no manufacturing capacities in the pharmaceutical sector to import 
pharmaceutical products at affordable prices.

Credit, the issue was referred to Reserve Bank of India who advised that 
a Bank Guarantee is issued by a bank in favour of a beneficiary of the 
performance of certain acts by the customers of the banks in the form of 
a performance guarantee or a financial guarantee and is general in nature 
and cannot replace Letter of Credit mechanism as detailed in ICC Uniform 
Customs and Practice for Documentary Credit (UCP 500). A Letter of 
Credit is always trade related and opened by the buyer of goods favouring 
seller indicating the terms of the contract fulfilment of which enables the 
seller to receive payment form the bank in his country without waiting for 
the payment by buyer. A buyer may settle for a bank guarantee if he has 
confidence in the supplier. For the purpose of extending benefits, however, 
no distinction may be made between bank guarantee and L/C, as both 
are treated as securities for receivables.

modify or relax the existing provisions since the irrevocable L/C is time

Awareness for TB Control 
1268. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that four out of every ten Indians are infected 
by mycobacterium tuberculosis and five to ten per cent of them finally 
get the disease; 
(b) if so, the steps taken to ar rest the spread of tuberculosis 
especially when it is highly infectious and being airborne the bacteria 
cut across all age groups and socio-economic barriers; and 
(c) whether Government propose to launch any special drive with 
a view to educating masses about the preventive and curative aspects 
of tuberculosis specially in tribal, adivasi and backward areas like 
Yavatmal in Maharashtra? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI 
SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) To control the disease, the National TB Control Programme has 
been in operation in the country si nce 1962. The Revised National TB 
Control Programme (RNTCP) based on DOTS, which is a WHO 
recommended strategy, was launched in 1993 and is being implemented 
in a phased manner, with the objective of achieving cure rate of 85% of 
new sputum positive cases. Diagnosi s by sputum microscopy instead 
of by X-ray helps in detecting and curing infectious cases on priority. 
Facilities for diagnosis by sputum microscopy have been decentralized 
and strengthened. Drugs are provided free of cost in patient-wise boxes 
and patients are monitored so that they complete their treatment. The 
project districts have reported a cure rate of more than 80% which 
means more that 8 out of every 10 patients diagnosed and put on 
treatment under revised strategy are successfully treated. This is double 
96 

[15 December, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
that of the earlier programme. The death rates have also reduced from 
29% to 4%. DOTS coverage is being rapidly expanded in the country. 
From 20 million coverage in 1998,  about 760 million population has 
been covered at present. It is envisaged to cover 850 million population 
by 2004 under the revised strategy  and the entire population of the 
country by 2005. 
(c) IEC activity, is one of the im portant components of TB control 
strategy. Facts about TB and DO's and DON'Ts are published in the 
leading national newspapers from time to time. Similarly, State/Districts 
TB Societies also publish the same in the regional and local newspapers. 
IEC prototype material has been developed at the Central level and given 
to the State to translate into the local language. The Districts plan IEC 
activities as per local requirement and use locally available media to 
create awareness among the masses, including backward and tribal areas. 
Districts have been advised to ensure wall paintings in microscopy and 
DOT centres and at prominent places to convey the message that TB is 
fully curable if full course of treatment is taken and that all diagnosis and 
treatment facilities are provided free of cost. Bunds for undertaking IEC 
activities are provided under the programme.

THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI 
SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) As per feedback available from State Drugs 
Control Administrations, 36947, 34574 and 36314 drug samples were 
tested during the period 2000-2001, 2001-2002 and 2002-2003, out of 
which 112,98 and 125 samples respectively were found purious. Thus, it

(b) and (c) Under the Drugs & Cosmetics Act, 1940 and rules there 
under, the responsibility for regulating manufacture and sale of drugs 
including taking administrative and legal action against the manufacturers 
rests with the State Governments. Based on the gravity of the offence 
detected, necessary punitive action under the said Act and Rules is 
taken against manufacturers for such categories of drugs by the concerned 
Drugs Controllers. In view of this, specific details of spurious drug detected 
etc. together with their identified manufacturers are, not maintained 
centrally. 
(d) and (e): Under the provisions  of Drugs & Cosmetics Act, 1940 
and Rules thereunder, the responsibility for regulating manufacture and 
sale of drugs including monitoring t heir quality is vested with the State 
Government. The State Governments are advised from time to time to 
gear up their enforcement machinery to detect and unearth spurious/ 
99 

RAJYA SABHA [15 December, 2003] 
fake drugs moving in the inter-state commerce as well as to provide and 
strengthen their regulatory infrastruc ture; to establish their own State 
level testing labs, to ensure speedy analysis of drug samples for which 
they are provided assistance to strengthen and augment their labs and 
infrastructure facilities. The State Governments have also been advised 
to keep strict surveillance over the suspected dealers; collection of survey 
samples under NSQD programme; constitution/reactivation of state drug 
advisory committees in which various trade and industry association as 
well as consumer associations can file representations; establishment 
of separate intelligence-cum-legal cell; development of efficient 
communication facilities and recall procedures; engaging experienced 
counsel for fighting spurious drug cases etc. 
Government of India has taken the following initiatives to tackle 
the problem of spurious drugs:- 
i) Detailed guidelines in respect of strategies required to be adopted 
for efficient surveillance over t he movement of spurious drugs 
were issued to states in November 17, 1999 to ensure focused 
surveiuance over manufacture and sale of spurious drugs. 
ii) The issue of alleged sale of spurious drugs was taken up by Union 
Health Minister with State Health Ministers in the 7th Conference 
of Central Council of Health (CCH) & FW held on 12-13 July, 
2001. CCH resolved that in order to address issues relating to 
the increasing reports of spurious drugs/counterfeit drug, special 
attention requires to be given to monitor and unearth such illegal 
activities by constituting a separate intelligence-cum-legal cell in 
the respective drug control organization and in seeking 
cooperation of the pharma industry, trade as well as the police. 
iii) Department of Health constituted a broad based Committee under 
the Chairmanship of DGHS in July, 2001 to examine issue 
concerning the problem of spurious drugs. The observation and 
recommendations of this Committee have been circulated on 
September 16, 2002 to all State Drugs Controllers for their 
information and necessary action in the matter. 
iv) Union Minister of Health and Family Welfare had specifically written 
to all Chief Ministers on Oct., 8, 2002 on the issue of spurious

SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) and (b) Tuberculosis and AIDS/HIV are major 
public health problem in the country. 
108 

[15 December, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
About 18 lakh new cases of TB are occurring every year. To control 
the disease, the National TB Control Programme has been in operation in 
the country since 1962. The Revise d National TB Control Programme 
(RNTCP) based on DOTS, which is a WHO recommended strategy 
was introduced in 1993 and is being implemented in a phased manner, 
with the objective of achieving cure rate of 85% of new sputum positive 
cases. Diagnosis by sputum microscopy instead of X-ray helps in 
detecting and curing infectious cases on priority. Facilities for diagnosis 
by sputum microscopy have been decentralized and strengthened. 
Drugs are provided free of cost in patient-wise boxes and patients are 
monitored so that they complete their treatment. 
The project districts have reported a cure rate of more than 80% 
which means more than 8 out of every 10 patients diagnosed and put on 
treatment under the revised strategy are successfully treated. This is 
double that of the earlier programme.

million coverage in 1998, about 750 million population has been covered 
at present. It is envisaged to cover 650 million population by 2004 under 
the revised strategy and the entire population of the country by 2005.' 
To make the programme more accessible to large segments of the 
population and to supplement the Government efforts in this direction, 
emphasis is being given to also involve medical colleges, all general 
hospitals, private practitioners and NGOs in the programme. 
In order to prevent and control the spread of HIV/AIDS in India, Govt, 
of India has launched a comprehensive National AIDS Control Programme, 
currently under implementation throughout the country as a centrally 
sponsored scheme under following components:- 
— Preventive interventions for high-risk populations through targeted 
interventions adopting a multi-pr onged strategy including peer 
counselling, treatment of Sexually Transmitted Infections and 
Behaviour Change Communication. 
— Preventive interventions for the general population through 
programmes for Blood Safety, Voluntary Counselling and Testing 
Services, Prevention of Parent to Child Transmission Services, 
Information Education and Communication (IEC) & awareness

building among adolescents and sensitization for the AIDS Vaccine

— Provision of low cost care and support services by providing 
community care services, treatment  of opportunistic infections 
and prevention of occupational exposure. 
— Collaborative efforts to promot e inter-sectoral co-ordination 
activities including workplace interventions and public-private 
partnerships. 
Building technical and managerial capacities for programme 
implementation through surveillance, training, monitoring and evaluation, 
technical resource groups, oper ational research and programme 
management.

(b) to (d) The measures undertaken to detect spurious drugs by the

Statement 
The Drugs Control Department, Govt, of NCT of Delhi takes the 
following routine measures to contain the problems of spurious 
drugs:— 
1. Routine inspections/special inspections and raids in the 
manufacturing premises and sale outlets are carried out from time 
to time. Officers of Drugs Control Department, Govt, of India, are 
also sometimes associated in such raids and special inspections. 
2. Legal samples (samples drawn under the Act) are being taken at 
randum from all the licensed drugs manufacturing units, sales 
establishments, hospitals, dispensaries and medical stores 
throughout Delhi including the far-flung areas and JJ Colonies. 
During current financial year (upto 30.11.2003), a total no. of 1182 
samples have been collected and out of the samples tested so 
far, none has been reported to be spurious. 
3. Survey samples of drugs are drawn at random to have a test 
check on the quality of drugs moving in the market. Survey samples 
of drugs are test purchased through decoy customers and watchers 
from chemists in Delhi and are got screened immediately. In case 
there is doubt or the active ingredients are found absent, the 
premises from where the samples were taken are raided and legal 
samples of the concerned drug are taken for test and analysis, if 
available, for taking appropriate action against the dealer under 
the provisions Drugs & Cosmetics Act, 1940. During the current 
financial year (upto 30.11.2003) a total no. of 2204 survey samples 
have been collected. All these samples passed the 'identification 
test' for active medicament. 
4. Complaints received in the department about quality of drugs are 
investigated immediately and appropriate action are taken. 
5. Activities of person of doubtful nature are kept under surveillance. 
116 

[15 December, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
6. Liaison is maintained with local police to check and stop 
movements of drugs of doubtful quality through unauthorized and 
illicit channels. 
7. Close liaison is also maintained with the manufacturers and dealers 
of repute with a view to obtaining information against movement, 
if any, of drugs of doubtful quality. 
8. An Advisory Committee has been constituted by the department 
to increase the public participation for efficient enforcement. The 
Committee consists of repres entatives of India Medical 
Association, Delhi Medical Asso ciation, All India Small Scale 
Pharmaceuticals Manufacturers Association (Delhi Branch), 
Chemists Associations and Voluntary Consumers Forums. 
The Department has given wide publicity to the DO's and DONT's for 
consumers through pamphlets and advertisements in the leading 
newspapers including insistence by consumer for issue of cash memo 
by the chemists. Advertisements in leading dailies has also been 
published instructing the dealers to confirm to the requirements of Drugs 
and Cosmetics Rules while selling drugs.

Deaths due to TB 
1289. DR. AKHILESH DAS: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that despite all efforts made in pursuance of 
the National Health Policy, at least one man succumbs every minute due 
to the ghastly disease, tuberculosis in the country; 
(b) if so, the number of TB caused deaths and the number of new TB 
cases registered during 2001,2002 and 2003; so far, State-wise; and 
(c) the specific steps taken for eradication and control of TB during 
these years? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI 
SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) and (b) As per WHO Global Annual TB 
Surveillance Report. It is estimated that about 4.17 lac patients die of 
TB every year in the country i.e. about 1/minute. The details of the 
deaths reported during the last three years in the areas implementing 
RNTCP are given in the enclosed Statement-I (See below) and number 
of new TB cases registered under the Programme are given in the 
enclosed Statement-ll (Seebelow). 
122 

[15 December, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
(c)The National TB Control Programme was in operation in the country 
since 1962. However, this progra mme could not achieve the desired 
results. Therefore, the Revised National TB Control Programme (RNTCP) 
widely known as DOTS, which is a WHO recommended strategy, is 
being implemented in a phased manner, with the objective of achieving 
cure rate of 85% of new sputum po sitive cases. Diagnosis by sputum 
microscopy instead of by X-ray helps in detecting and curing infectious 
cases on priority,. Facilities for di agnosis by sputum microscopy have 
been decentralized and strengthened. Drugs are provided under 
supervision and patients are monitored so that they complete their 
treatment. Drugs are provided free of cost in patient-wise boxes. 
The project districts have reported a cure rate of more than 80% 
which means more than 8 out of every 10 patients diagnosed and put on 
treatment under the revised strategy are successfully treated. This is 
double that of the earlier programme. TB death rates have reduced from 
29% to 4%. 
DOTS coverage is being rapidly expanded in the country. From 20 
million coverage in 1998, about 760 million population has been covered 
at present. It is envisaged to cover 850 million population by 2004 under 
the revised strategy and the entire population of the country by 2005.

Admission in Medical Colleges 
1292. SHRI V. NARAYANASAMY: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the fact that the Supreme Court 
in its recent judgement ordered reservation of 50 per cent seats to the 
State quota for admission in the Medical Colleges in MBBS course; 
(b) whether it is a fact that the Supreme Court further ordered that 
the State should be given power in fixing fees, monitoring of admissions, 
and the connected matters; and 
(c) if so, whether Government have implemented the order of the 
Supreme Court earnestly? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI 
SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) to (c) The Hon'ble Supreme Court in its judgement 
dated 14.8.2003 in the case of Islamic Academy of Education and another 
vs. State of Karnataka and others has directed that the different 
percentage of quota for students to be admitted by the management in 
each minority or non-minority unaid ed professional colleges shall be 
separately fixed on the basis of their need by the respective State 
127 

RAJYA  SABHA [15 December, 2003] 
Governments. The remaining seats shall be filled up by the State agencies 
themselves. However, for the academic year 2003-04 as the outer time 
limit for admission of students was fast approaching or had gone, as a 
temporary arrangement the Hon'ble Cour t directed that the seats be 
filled by the institution and the State Governments in the ratio of 50:50. 
In the aforesaid judgement, the Hon'ble Court also directed that the 
respective State Governments shall set up two separate Committee 
headed by a retired High Court judge who shall be nominated by the 
Chief Justice of the concerned State. While the Hon'ble Court has clarified 
that each private institute shall have the freedom to fix its own fee 
structure, one of the above said Committees would decide whether the 
fees proposed by the institute concerned are justified and are profiteering 
or charging capitation fee. The fee fixed by the Committee shall be binding 
on the institute for a period of three years. 
The Hon'ble Court has further directed that the management could 
select students, of their quota, either on the basis of the common entrance 
tests conducted by the State or on the basis of the common entrance 
test to be conducted by an association of all colleges of a particular type 
in that State, e.g. medical, engineering etc. The second Committee, which 
required to be set up by each State Government, shall ensure that the 
tests conducted by the association of colleges is fair and transparent.

Blindness Control 
1295. SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Will the Minister 
of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether India has the dubious distinction of having the largest 
number of blind persons in the world; and 
(b) if so, the measures taken to improve serious health problems of 
people affected by blindness? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) As per WHO estimates, there 
are 45 million blind persons in the world out of which nearly 7 million blind 
persons are in India. 
(b) Following measures are being taken to prevent and control 
blindness and restore vision of the affected population: 
1. Free Cataract Surgery at Government Hospitals and by Voluntary 
Organisations. 
2. Screening of children with refractive errors and provisions of 
corrective glasses. 
3. Collection and transplantation of  donated eyes for treatment of 
corneal blindness. 
4. Public awareness for prevention and treatment of Eye ailments.

peripheral units, evaluating the performance of the Targeted Interventions,

Surveys among general population and high-risk groups, involvement of

Baseline Behavioural Surveys, an external agency M/s. ORG Marg was 
hired after going through an International Competitive Bidding (ICB) 
process to ensure that an external  agency conduct this activity, 
impartially, as per the guidelines.

1303. PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM: Will the Minister of HEALTH

(a) whether it is a fact that India is on the verge of coming out with 
AIDS vaccine;

a vaccine at affordable price?

AIDS scare in Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu 
1316. SHRI SANJAY NIRUPAM: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that as per  the latest report of WHO, four 
million to five million people are infected with HIV in India and UNAIDS-
WHO report speaks to "serious epi demics" underway in Maharashtra 
and Tamil Nadu; 
(b) if so. the details thereof; and 
161 

RAJYA SABHA [15 December, 2003] 
(c) the steps taken to overcome the crisis? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI 
SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) and (b) The National AIDS Control 
Organisation, Government of India conducts a nation-wide HIV sentinel 
surveillence each year, in order to monitor the trends and to estimate 
the burden of HIV infection in the country. The estimated number of people 
living with HIV is 3.82 million at the lower end of the range and 4.58 
million at the higher end. The States of Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu are 
among the six high prevalance States for HIV/AIDS. The others 4 high 
prevalence States are Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Manipur and Nagaland. 
(c) In order to prevent and control the spread of HIV/AIDS in India, 
Government of India has launched a comprehensive National AIDS Control 
Programme, currently under implementation throughout the country as a 
centrally sponsored scheme with the following components:— 
• Preventive interventions for high-risk populations through targeted 
interventions adopting a multi-pr onged strategy including peer 
counselling and behaviour change communication. 
• Preventive interventions for the general population through 
programmes for blood safety, voluntary, counselling and testing 
services, Prevention of parent to Child Transmission (PPTCT), 
treatment of Sexually Transmitt ed Diseases (STD), Information 
Education and Communication (IEC) and awareness building 
among adolescents and sensitization for the AIDS Vaccine 
Initiative. 
• Provision of low cost care and support services by providing 
community care services, treatment  of opportunistic infections 
and prevention of occupational exposure. 
• Collaborative efforts to promote inter-sectoral programme activities 
including workplace interventions and public-private partnerships. 
• Building technical and managerial capacities for programmes 
implementation through Surveillance, Training, Monitoring the 
Evaluation, Technical resource, groups, operational research 
and Programme management. 
In addition, two projects namely AIDS  Prevention  and Control 
162 

[15 December, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
Project (APAC), in Tamil Nadu and AVERT in Maharashtra are under 
implementation for effective prevention and control of HIV/AiDS in these 
States. These projects are suppo rted by United State Agency for 
International Development (USAID).

contaminants during 1986-91 and published a report in 1993. The report 
was however, withdrawn in 1994 due to deficiency in the methodology 
adopted. 
On the basis of the advice of the ex perts, the permissible limits of 
food additives and pesticides have been reviewed from time to time. 
The Ministry of Agriculture has also  constituted expert committees to 
review the health of safety of different pesticides and banned/restricted 
use of some of the pesticides. Keeping in view the residue of pesticides 
in different components including foods items, the Government of India 
is advocating Integrated Pest Management (IPM) which inter alia includes 
the cultural, mechanical biological and need based judicious use of 
pesticides, use of bio-pesticides banning/phasing out the most persistent 
organochlorine group of pesticides, educating the farmers on judicious 
use of pesticides and observance of waiting period, encouraging organic 
farming etc.

1. Review/Repeal of obsolete laws:

particular to secure:-

disposal of cases without affect ing the cardinal principle that 
decisions should be just and fair.

and devices for delay so that it operates not as an end in itself 
but as a means of achieving justice.

[15 December, 2003] RAJYA SABHA

tion of justice.

suggest such legislation as might be necessary to implement the Directive 
Principles and to attain the objective set out in the Preamble to the 
Constitution.

6.To recommend to the Government measure for bringing the statute 
book up-to-date by repealing obsolete laws and enactments or parts 
thereof which have outlived their utility.- 
7.To consider and to convey to the Government its views on any 
subject relating to law and judicial administration that may be referred to

The present Law. Commission consists of a Chairman, a Vice-
Chairman and a part-time Member. The present Chairman is a retired 
Judge of the Hon'be Supreme Court of India. The present Vice-Chairman 
and part-time Member are Legal Experts. 
(b) The various Law Commissions constituted from time to time 
submitted a number of reports on Indian Penal Code and related laws 
including the laws relating to Crime against Women. In addition to the 
various recommendations made by the law Commission relating to these 
subjects in earlier reports, on the request of Central Government, the 
Law Commission of India undertook a comprehensive review of the 
Indian Penal Code 1860 and submitted its 156th report. In its 156th 
report, the Law Commission of India has focused its attention on the 
lapsed Indian Penal Code (amendment) Bill 1978 and endorsed many 
of the proposal containing the lapsed Indian Penal Code (amendment) 
Bill 1978. Some more recommendations were made by the Law 
Commission on the subject in its 172nd, 177th, and 178th report. The 
major recommendations contained in  these reports of the Law 
Commission are as follows:- 
(i) To make the offence punishable under section 290, 298, 
431,432,434,504,505,and 510 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 
cognizable. 
199 

RAJYA SABHA [15 December, 2003] 
(ii) Amount of fine provided in various sections of the Indian Penal 
Code to be increased at least by 20 times and also to make a 
provision in the Cr. P.C. regarding powers of the First Class 
Magistrate to impose such a fine. 
(iii) Enhancement of the period of the imprisonment provided under 
section 354 of the Indian Penal Code regarding assualt and 
criminal force to women with the intent to outrage her modesty 
from two years to five years. 
(iv) The period of imprisonment provided under section 509 IPC 
regarding uttering any word or making any gesture intended to 
insult the modesty of the woman etc. to be enhanced from one 
year to three years. 
(v) In the light of surfacing of va rious sort of financial scams in 
various fields like banks, hospita ls, non-financial institutions 
involving crores of rupees, the Law Commission has 
recommended insertion of new section 120BB in the Indian 
Penal Code, 1860 to tackle the problem. 
To deal with the issue of increasing sexual violence on women and 
female children, the law commission recommends that the offence of 
sexual assult be added to the existing offence of outraging the modesty 
of women in section 354 and punishme nt be increased from two years 
to five years. Accordingly, Section 354 be amended on the following 
lines:- 
"354. Assault or criminal force to woman with intent to outrage her 
modesty-whoever assaults or uses criminal force to any woman, 
intending to outrage her modesty or to commit sexual assault to 
her or knowing it to be likely that he will thereby outrage her modesty 
or commit sexual assault to her, shall be punished with imprisonment 
or either description for a term which may extend to five years and 
shall also be liable to fine." 
Expanding the scope of Section 35 4 in the above manner, would 
cover the varied forms of sexual violence other than rape on women and 
female children. 
200 

[15 December, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
The Law Commission is further of the view that the offence of eve 
teasing falls within the scope of Section 509 and there is no need for a 
new Section 376F as recommended by the National Commission for 
Woman. However, the Law Commission feels that the quantum of 
punishment be increased from one year to three years and fine. 
Accordingly, it is recommended that Section 509 be amended in 
the following manner: 
"Section 509: whoever, intending to insult the modesty of any 
women, utters any word, makes any sound or gesture, or exhibits 
any object, intending that such word or sound shall be heard or that 
such gesture or object shall be se e, by such woman, or intrudes 
upon the privacy of such woman, shall be punished with 
imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to 3 
years and shall also be liable to fine" 
(c) and (d) The recommendations of the Law Commission made in

and the views of the State Governme nts are in the process of being

Notification of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1995 
1377. SHRI K. RAHMAN KHAN: 
DR. AKHILESH DAS: 
Will the Minister of URBAN DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY 
ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether, in view of the rec ent, Supreme Court order on giving 
effect to the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1995, Government have taken any 
decision to notify the date of enforcement of the Act with a view to carrying 
out mandate of the Parliament; 
(b) if so, the decision taken in the matter; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI BANDARU 
DATTATRAYA): (a) to (c) The Suprem e Court, in its judgement dated 
8.10.2003 dismissed Civil Appeals Nos. 3988-89 of 2001 filed by Common 
Cause for issuing order to the Central Government to notify the Delhi 
Rent Control Act, 1995. In the sa id judgement the Supreme Court 
observed that the Government is entitled to take into consideration various 
facts while deciding whether the Act should be brought into force or not 
and no mandamus can be issued to the Central Government to bring the 
Act into force. 
The Delhi Rent Control Act, 1995 could not be enforced after its 
enactment due to agitation by various groups. It was then decided to bring 
the Act into force after amending some of its provisions. Consequently, 
224 

[15 December, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
the Delhi Rent Control (Amendment) Bill, 1997 was introduced in the Rajya 
Sabha on 28.7.1997.The same was referred to the Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Urban and Rural Development for examination and report. 
The Committee has since submitted its report and its recommendations 
have also been accepted by the Government. After the Amendment Bill is 
passed in both the Houses of Parliament and assented to by the President, 
the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1995 alongwith the amendments can be brought 
into force.

1386. SHRI NANDI YELLAIAH: W ill the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of the Valmiki Ambedkar Awas Yojana and the categories 
of urban poor who are entitled to become beneficiaries of this scheme 
and the details of the rules and conditions under which the beneficiaries 
are provided with the constructed houses; 
(b) the number of the beneficia ries under VAMBAY as on date, 
State-wise; and 
(c) the amount released so far under this scheme, and the locations 
for which the funds had been released so far, State-wise? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI BANDARU 
DATTATRAYA): (a) Valmiki Ambedkar Awas Yojana is a Centrally Sponsored 
Scheme with a funding pattern on a 50:50 ratio between Centre and the 
States. The scheme is primarily aimed at ameliorating the housing problems 
for the slum dwellers living below poverty line including members of 
economically weaker section who do not possess adequate shelter. This 
scheme has also a component called Nirmal Bharat Abhiyan to provide 
healthy and enabling urban environment in urban slums through community 
sanitation. As per the extant guidelines, Scheduled Caste/Tribe, Backward 
classes, other weaker sections and physically and mentally disabled persons 
residing in slums are entitled for the benefits under the scheme. Beneficiaries 
are identified while formulating the project itself and the constructed houses 
are handed over to them on completion of the project.

VAMBAY as on 30.11.2003 are given at Annexure-l.The State-wise locations

1387. SHRI RAMADHAR KASHYAP: Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a num ber of plots sold by DDA through 
auction in Vikash Puri, New Delhi over twenty years ago have not 
been constructed/build up till date; 
(b) why the DDA/MCD is not taking appropriate action in the matter; 
and 
(c) the reasons for which DDA/MCD is allowing such plots to be 
used as garbage sites creating unhygienic conditions for the residents of 
the area? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATIOM (SHRI BANDARU 
DATTATRAYA): (a) to (c) Delhi Development Authority (DDA) has reported 
that in case of plots sold in auction, the possession is handed over to the 
auction purchaser after payment of the total bid amount and the purchasers 
are allowed a period of two years for construction from the date of 
241 

RAJYA SABHA [15 December, 2003] 
possession. As per the terms and conditions of lease, the purchaser is 
required to construct the building after obtaining sanction of the building 
plan from concerned local authority. There may be some cases where 
the auction purchasers have not completed the construction on plots 
allotted to them. Delhi Development Authority charges composition fee 
from the auction purchaser for non-c onstruction of the building on the 
plot. 
After the possession is handed over to the purchaser, it is his 
responsibility to protect the plot  from any unauthorized use. Delhi 
Development Authority does not allow any person to utilize the plot as 
garbage site.

export routes through Arunachal Pradesh 
SHRI NABAM REBIA (Arunachal Pradesh): Madam, my Special 
Mention relates to reopening of Indo-Myanmar, Indo-China and Indo-

South East Asia were accessible by 1,736 kms.-long Stilwell Road from 
Ledo in Assam via Jairampur in Arunachal Pradesh, Myitkyina in Myanmar 
to Kunming in Yunnan province of China. This historical road, constructed 
during the World War-ll by the Armed Forces, in the present context 
could be a gateway to trans-border trade, promotion to tourism and re-
establishing the socio-cultural ties.

Return' in Myanmar, Pangsau Pass and War Cemetery at Jairampur in 
Arunachal Pradesh are important landmarks just along the Arunachal-
Myanmar Border, which in the present context will, no doubt, be a 
favoured tourist destination, benefiting Arunachal Pradesh and Assam. 
Urgent need to tackle tuberculosis in the country 
SHRI R. KAMARAJ (Tamil Nadu): Madam, I wish to bring to the 
notice of the Government the urgent need to tackle the tuberculosis time 
bomb that is ticking away. India ha s the dubious distinction of being 
home to the world's largest number of tuberculosis patients. It is estimated 
that half of the tuberculosis patients in our country are in the economically 
productive age-group of 15 to 44. Though many treatment methods to 
this disease were developed both at the global and the national levels, 
the disease keeps developing new resistant forms. This posses a serious 
261 

RAJYA  SABHA [15 December, 2003] 
problem in handling this disease. The Indian experience in 
tuberculosis control has two dimension to it, research and treatment. 
Though there has been a lot of input in terms of research, it seems the 
nation has not made use of the advances made in the area of 
treatment. The Revised National Tuberculosis Control Programme, 
covering 221 districts in 21 States, is said to have averted more than 
1.5 lakh deaths. Yet, the disease continues to take its toll. As the 
menace posed by tuberculosis is of a massive dimension, there will be 
no real success until the most important segment of the medical 
system, the private sector, is involv ed in controlling it. Because of the 
inadequacies in the public healthcare system, half of the patients seek 
the services of private healthcare service providers. So, in order to 
tackle this ticking time-bomb called "tuberculosis" and save our 
citizens, I request the Central Government to revamp the healthcare 
system without delay. Thank you.

Need to initiate relief measures to boost the coffee industry in the 
country 
SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA (Karna taka): Madam, my Special 
Mention is about the need for initiating relief measures to boost coffee 
industry in our country. Our country is one of the major producers of 
coffee in the world. As per the latest data of the Ministry of Commerce, 
production of coffee in the country in 1999-2000 was 2,92,000 metric 
tons; in 2000-2001, it was 3,01,200 metric tons; and in 2001-2002, it 
was 3,06,000 metric tons. As against that, the domestic consumption 
of coffee for the same period was 55,000 metric tons, 60,000 metric 
tons and 64,000 metric tons respectively. My home State, Karnataka, 
tops in the production of coffee. But it is a matter of concern that the 
production of coffee in Karnataka is on a decline. It was 2,10,950 
metric tons in 2000-2001, 2,08,670 metric tons in 2001 -2002 and 
1,91,300 metric tons in 2002-2003. These trends are very much 
disturbing. No doubt, drought has bro ught down production, but it is 
equally true that coffee growers have lost interest in the production 
due to unremunerative prices both in international and domestic 
markets. In the international market, the coffee prices have nose-dived 
due to stiff competition from Vietnam and other coffee producing 
countries. The domestic market too is very sluggish. There are no 
takers of coffee resulting in severe setback to the coffee industry. 
The Government and the Coffee Board are implementing various 
schemes for coffee growers including special coffee term loans, 
reduction in interest rate by one per cent on such loans, etc. But that is 
not enough to boost the coffee industry unless it becomes remunerative 
for which production has to be increased by expanding cultivation areas; 
the cost of production which is very high has to be reduced by innovative 
technology; new international markets are to be found and coffee has to 
be popularised in the domestic mark et through systematic campaigns 
and coffee growers, particularly the smaller ones have to be given interest 
free loans and other incentives. I, t herefore, urge the Government to 
save the coffee industry, particularly in Karnataka. Thank you.

Plight of weavers in the country 
MISS MABEL REBELLO (Madhya Pradesh): Sir, by the end of 2004, 
the Multi-Fibre Agreement, which pr ovided for quotas for exports for 
different countries, would come to an end. Textiles form the single biggest 
commodity exported from the country and it is also the second biggest 
provider of employment after agriculture. There is, therefore, 
understandable anxiety as to how things would shape up for the country 
from January, 2005. The development of the sector would be highly skewed 
269 

RAJYA SABHA [15 December, 2003] 
with thousands of small units in un-organised/de-centralised sector losing 
out from their positions. Textile Up-gradation Fund (TUF) has made very 
limited impact on this decentralised sub-sector. The larger units in the 
organised sector have taken the bulk of cheap credit under the TUF and 
most of the single-loom owners or small units have not been able to 
benefit from the scheme. The picture turns bleaker with the removal of 
Quantitative Restrictions on imports coupled with reduction in duties on 
imports of yarns, fibres and textile products in recent years. The import 
of all these textile items has risen sharply and India's textile sector with 
its out-dated machinery and slower production systems finds it difficult 
to hold on in the world market with ultra modern machinery and higher/ 
faster production systems. The Government must prepare a realistic plan 
of modernization which is focused on the decentralised sector in order to 
work out how many existing weavers can be absorbed on modern looms, 
how many would be without their jobs and then prepare plans for 
rehabilitating them.

Need to stop misuse of disposable syringes in the country 
SHRI B.J. PANDA (Orissa): Sir, thank you for permitting me to raise 
this important issue of serious menance of disposable syringes. 
Sir, disposable syringes are found scattered alongside bandages, 
infected human body parts and staine d cotton balls in dumps on the 
backyard of the hospitals. In the dead of night, scavengers make their 
way to the dump and collect these infected piece of plastic, sell them to 
kabariwalas who pass them on to unscrupulous re-packagers and soon 
these disposable syringes make their way to nursing homes. Infected 
syringes are believed to be signific ant contributors to the spread of 
infections like HIV and Hepatitis-B. The World Health Organisation 
estimates that between 80,000 and 1,60,000 people are infected because 
of unsafe injections which are wholly preventable. India has the second 
largest pool of Hepatitis-B carriers  in the world. Studies conducted 
worldwide show a direct co-relati on between the reuse of syrings and 
spread of infection. In our country, we have a mind-set of recycling. It is 
found that clandestine operators put disposable syringes to use again 
without dis-infection. The world over the trend is to move towards single 
use, auto-disabled syringes, which break or jam after onetime use.These 
auto-disabled syringes are, however, not manufactured in/our country. 
Sir, 85 per cent of health care services in our country are in private hands

this Bill in its present form and it will really lose the development character

Bank Bill, 2002. Now, we all know that IDBI was created in 1964 and later

subscribed to its entire share capital. After Independence, our country

coordinating the working of the institutions engaged in financing, promoting or 
developing industry, and, assisting the development of such institutions. Madam, 
initially, IDBI was set up as a wholly-owned subsidiary of the Reserve Bank of 
India. In 1976, the entire share holding of the IDBI was transferred to the 
Central Government. Subsequently, the IDBI Act was amended in 1994, 
which, interalia enabled the IDBI to enlarge its shareholder's base and access 
the capital market for resources. It is noteworthy to mention that due to 
enlargement of shareholder's base, the shareholding of the Central 
Government has become 58.5%. 
The flow of funds to financial institutions from Reserve Bank of India's 
National Industrial Credit Long Term Operations and allocation of Statutory 
Liquidity Ratio bonds dried up and it became necessary for the financial 
institutions to raise funds mainly from the markets. 
The Narasimhan Committee suggested that the financial institutions should 
convert ultimately into commercial banks or non-banking financial companies. 
The Khan Working Group set up by the Reserve Bank of India also 
recommended that Development Financial Institutions should be allowed to 
convert into banks at the earliest. 
The present Bill seeks to provide the repealing of IDBI Act, 1964 and 
transfers the undertaking to the company to be formed under the 
Companies Act, 1956. Further allowing such company to carry on 
banking business in accordance with the provisions of the Banking 
Regulation Act, 1949. 
Before implementing the provisions of this Bill, the hon. Finance 
Minister should address the apprehension of the All India Industrial 
Development Bank Employees Association and the issues raised by the IDBI 
Workers Union and other economists vis-a-vis the implications of the 
proposed amendments. 
291 

RAJYA SABHA [15 December, 2003] 
They are of the view that new corporate entity will not be viable 
without the Government's support and many economists also 
substantiated this view, the IDBI should be allowed to function as a 
Development Financial Institution in the national interest as it is the 
last such institution in the country. 
We should analyse their demand in comparison with other countries. 
All developed and developing countries world-wide do have such.institution 
for development of industry and employment generation. 
Further, Development Financial Inst itution is not profit-oriented; 
IDBI has got only a social objective. The social objective was to develop 
industries, generate employment and distribute industrial development 
equitably in different States of the country. 
It is noteworthy to mention that Japan has created a Government-
owned Development Financial Institut ion in 1999 to contribute to the 
implementation of economic and social policy. 
Their reasonable contention is social objective which is not possible 
for a company or a commercial bank which is mainly profit-oriented 
and our country is left out with no Development Financial Institution. 
The other causing concern is if IDBI becomes a banking company, 
its employees may be required to possess specific professional skills 
and they may also be required to be posted in new locations as the 
bank expands its network. Some employees may not be able to cope up 
with such situations or requirement s. This would compel them to opt 
not be in the service of the company, because in pursuance of this provision 
of the Bill, it will be considered as  if they have resigned. My humble 
suggestion is that a special VRS package should be launched for the 
present employees fo IDBI, so t hat no employee of any category is 
aggrieved due to its conversion into a banking company. 
Before implementing the provisions of this Bill, the above mentioned 
apprehensions of various quarters need to be addressed in clear terms. 
With these observations, I conclude.

SHRI P. G. NARAYANAN (Tamil Nadu): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, from 
the time the economic liberalisation of the Indian economy began, the 
successive Governments have been expanding the scope of future 
trading in India. The present Bill is to assess the role of the Forward 
Markets Commission. 
The Government had constituted a Committee in June, 1993, under 
the Chairmanship of Prof. K.N. Kabra, a Professor of the Indian Institute 
of Public Administration, to review the operations of forward markets and 
to assess the role of the Forward Markets Commission.

[15 December, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
The Committee submitted its proposals for amending the Forward 
Contracts Act, 1952, to strengthen the Forward Markets Commission as 
also arrangements for trading. 
The Forward Markets Commission regulates commodity futures 
trading in India. Its role is identical to that of Commodity Futures Trading 
Commission of the United States. 
The World Bank has acknowledge India's long experience in operating 
and managing commodity future markets. It has observed that restrictive 
policies have not provided India's agriculture future market a chance to 
contribute to price risk management and that the restrictive policies have 
discourged them from upgrading their institutional capabilities. 
Analysing all these, it is proposed to amend the existing Forward 
Contract (Regulations) Act, 1952. A modification of the definition of specific 
delivery contracts and non-transferable specific deliveries so as to make 
delivery of goods compulsory and to make perfornace of such a contract, 
by any means is, indeed, a welcome step. 
Further, it is proposed to define Future Contract and to provide for 
regulation in section 19, which needs to be addressed at length at the 
time of implementation. 
The implementing authorities should be very careful in recognising 
the dealings through brokers, in addition to the members of the commodity 
exchange, as there is always room for manipulations. 
These amendments are aimed at strengthening the existing 
systems and developing marketing systems that are consistent with the 
economic liberalisation and globalisat ion. With these submissions, I 
welcome this Bill. Thank you.

with the reply of the Government that the Government will have to move 
amendments for increasing the quantum of fine, time and again. In the 
opinon of the Committee, the quantum of fine should be fixed in accordance 
with the gravity of the offence. The executive should have the powers to 
change the same". The Committee, therefore, recommended that instead 
of qualifying the fine, the word as prescribed in the existing law, should 
be substituted so that the executive has the powers to change the same 
as and when required, instead of moving fresh amendments to the Act.

has to be further improved. I would also like that whatever observations 
have been made by the Standing Committee must have weightage in the 
Ministry. I hope, they will go through that, and will further improve it. With 
these words, I conclude, Sir.

STATEMENT BY MINISTER 
Action Against Indian Insurgent Groups Operating from Bhutan 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNA L AFFAIRS (SHRI YASHWANT 
SINHA): Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, we have been informed by the Royal 
Government of Bhutan th at they have launched today military action 
against Indian insurgent groups operating from camps in that country. 
The Government of India strongly supports this action of the Royal 
Government of Bhutan. 
His Majesty, the King of Bhutan,  had telephonically informed the 
Prime Minister of the impending action on Saturday, 13th December. 
The Prime Minister has conveyed to His Majesty, the King, that the 
Government and people of India stand firmly and solidly behind the Royal 
Government of Bhutan at this critic al juncture and would provide all 
necessary support as requested, till the task is completed. 
The Indian Army is also taking necessary measures to intercept 
movements of militants from Bhutan into India. 
The Government of India has adv ised the State Governments of 
Assam and West Bengal to remain alert to deal with the situation arising 
out of this action, including sealing the borders and maintaining peace. 
The Royal Government of Bhutan has always assured the Government 
of India that it will not allow its territory to be used for activities inimical to 
India's interest. The launch of operations against Indian insurgent groups 
in Bhutan has struck a blow against terrorism and terrorist activities in 
our entire region.

The action against Indian insurgent groups in Bhutan would prevent 
further loss of innocent lives by the mindless acts of violence perpetrated 
by these terrorists. It will promote peace, stability and security in the 
region and further cement the strong friendship and cooperation between 
India and Bhutan. Thank you.
